page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.ebmg9i.48xlarge is an ECS Bare Metal server instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It features 192 dedicated virtual CPUs powered by Intel Xeon 6982P-C processors running at a base clock speed of 3.2 GHz. The instance delivers a massive core count paired with 768.0 GB of system memory, maintaining a standard 1:4 CPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB RAM per core. Hardware virtualization is managed via KVM.

The hardware configuration does not bundle local disk storage, requiring external cloud storage volumes for all persistent OS and application data layers. It contains zero integrated GPU accelerators. Network connectivity provides a baseline bandwidth capacity of 64 Gbps, facilitating high-throughput node-to-node communication. Complimentary public IPv4 addresses are not included.

From an infrastructure efficiency perspective, the dedicated bare-metal deployment eliminates hypervisor overhead and resource contention across 192 cores. The large resource footprint is designed for heavy parallel computing, large enterprise databases, distributed container clusters, and demanding data analytics pipelines that require broad memory capacity and reliable non-virtualized processing power.
description: Alibaba Cloud ecs.ebmg9i.48xlarge is a dedicated bare-metal instance within the ECS Bare Metal family, built on the x86_64 architecture. It is powered by an Intel Xeon 6982P-C processor running at 3.2 GHz, delivering 192 dedicated vCPUs alongside 768.0 GB of system RAM. This configuration maintains a 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per core. The server includes no onboard local storage, necessitating remote block storage attachments for persistent filesystem requirements, and includes no discrete graphics processing units. Network interfaces support a baseline throughput of 64 Gbps without complimentary public IPv4 addresses. With full non-virtualized hardware access and KVM hypervisor integration, this server profile fits massive parallel processing workloads, large-scale distributed enterprise software, in-memory caching layers, and high-concurrency database deployments.
